extracted.intended_audience: Chemical manufacturers, importers, distributors, employers, SDS preparers, and regulatory compliance officers responsible for Hazard Communication Standard (HCS) compliance
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory requirements under OSHA's Hazard Communication Standard (HCS) about when and how manufacturers, importers, and distributors must classify hazards related to changes in physical form and chemical reaction products arising from known or reasonably anticipated downstream uses, and how to communicate those hazards on SDSs and labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufacturer responsibility for product classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturers of chemicals are responsible for the classification of their own chemical products.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA agrees manufacturers/importers/distributors are responsible for classifying their own products. They are not required to do hazard classification for downstream products unless they know or could reasonably anticipate the uses with sufficient information to classify. This is intended to avoid imposing duty to learn every downstream process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Upstream provision of sufficient hazard information
rubrics_metrics.description: Upstream manufacturers must provide sufficient hazard information about their own products so downstream users have the information they need to conduct their own hazard analyses and/or take other appropriate action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA clarified that the intent of paragraph (d)(1) is to ensure upstream manufacturers supply adequate hazard information for reasonably foreseeable uses so downstream employers/users can assess hazards and control measures; it is not to require upstream parties to perform downstream hazard analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold for classifying downstream hazards: known or reasonably anticipated uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturers need only classify hazards associated with known or reasonably anticipated uses, not every conceivable downstream use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA replaces 'under normal conditions of use and foreseeable emergencies' with requirement to include hazards associated with known and reasonably anticipated uses. The agency expects stakeholders to be familiar with 'known' and 'reasonably anticipated' from prior standards, guidance, and LOIs.

rubrics_metrics.name: SDS Section 2 content requirement for downstream hazards
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 2 of the SDS must contain information on hazards resulting from a change in the chemical's physical form and from chemical reaction products when they are known or can be reasonably anticipated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although there may be overlap with other sections, Section 2 is the appropriate location for information about actual hazards and specific hazard classifications that workers can easily access. Similar but different information may appear in Sections 5, 8, 10, 11, and 15 for other audiences/purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction of SDS sections by audience/purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 2 provides workers with easily understandable health and safety information; Section 10 provides technical information for designing safety systems; Section 5 provides fire-fighting measures; Section 8 provides exposure controls and personal protection (but not actual hazard identification); Section 11 provides stability and reactivity information mainly for medical/toxicology professionals; Section 15 is non-mandatory regulatory information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA explains the SDS format is standardized to improve usability; placing downstream-reaction hazard info in Section 2 ensures workers see actual hazards up-front while more technical info remains later in SDS.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labeling vs SDS — exclusion of downstream reaction hazards from shipped container labels
rubrics_metrics.description: Hazards resulting from a reaction with other chemicals under normal conditions of use do not have to be addressed on shipped container labels (HNOCs exclusion expanded to these hazards).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA believes inclusion of downstream reaction hazards on shipped-container labels could confuse users about immediate hazards; such hazards must still be included in Section 2 of the SDS and addressed in employee training where applicable. Labels and SDSs serve different purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: SDS presentation discretion to avoid warning fatigue
rubrics_metrics.description: SDS preparers have discretion to present information in Section 2 in an organized fashion to prevent confusion for downstream users and to avoid 'over-warning' or 'warning fatigue'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA is not dictating the format of presentation in Section 2, only requiring relevant hazard information be present; SDSs can contain comprehensive info appropriate for workers who need more details.

rubrics_metrics.name: OSHA alignment with GHS and international approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA interprets the GHS as applying to hazardous chemicals across life cycles and maintains authority to address national circumstances; OSHA's changes are consistent with GHS principles and similar international provisions that consider 'reasonably expected use'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA rejects argument that inclusion of downstream hazards on SDS diverges from GHS; it states other jurisdictions regulate shipped-chemical hazards and workplace hazards separately and that clarifying SDS obligations can strengthen international alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not requiring definition of 'reaction' in HCS
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA will not add a single definition of 'reaction' or 'chemical reaction' to paragraph (d)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA notes 'reaction' is used in multiple contexts throughout HCS; a single definition could create confusion. SDS preparers are expected to understand 'chemical reaction' as a change of chemical structure versus mere change in physical form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of dilution (mixing with water) and similar downstream uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Manufacturers would not be expected to classify hazards for actions like dilution with water that reduce chemical hazards and do not typically create new hazards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA explains that under finalized language, manufacturers need only classify hazards associated with known or reasonably anticipated uses; diluting a product with water generally reduces hazards and does not trigger additional classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation on upstream obligation — not required to learn every downstream process
rubrics_metrics.description: Upstream responsible parties are not required to learn the processes of every downstream user or perform hazard classification for each downstream process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA emphasizes that the duty to classify arises only when the manufacturer/importer/distributor knows or could reasonably anticipate the downstream use sufficiently to classify; this addresses concerns about duplicative or divergent downstream classifications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of narrowing classification only to label-specified or 'approved' uses
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA declines to limit classification obligations only to uses specified or directed by the upstream supplier, or only to 'approved' uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA finds such narrowing would reduce worker protections and could incentivize minimizing information on labels to avoid classification obligations; 'known and reasonably anticipated uses' is the appropriate standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: OSHA will not change 'article' definition or exemption status
rubrics_metrics.description: The changes in paragraph (d)(1) do not affect the HCS definition of 'article' or change the exemption status of any product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA clarifies that it did not intend to expand the HCS purview to include items previously treated as articles, and has revised proposed language to avoid such misinterpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer written hazard communication program access requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must develop, implement, maintain a written hazard communication program and make it available, upon request, to employees, their designated representatives, the Assistant Secretary, and the Director of NIOSH. The correct cross-reference is 29 CFR 1910.1020.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA corrected a typographical CFR reference (from §1910.20 to §1910.1020) and explains that §1910.1020 contains access requirements (reasonable time/place/manner, employer bears cost) appropriate for written hazard communication program records.

rubrics_metrics.name: SDS access vs copy — interplay with 1910.1020 exposure record rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The HCS requires immediate access to SDSs but does not itself require employers to provide copies; when an SDS constitutes an employee exposure record under 29 CFR 1910.1020(c)(5), the §1910.1020 access provisions (including opportunity to examine and copy) apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA declines to add a provision limiting copy requests to chemicals to which an employee was personally potentially exposed because that was beyond scope; where 1910.1020 applies, copying may be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Software/system feasibility and use of existing data sources
rubrics_metrics.description: SDS preparers and software systems can use the same sources used for classification of other chemicals as well as information from manufacturers to identify downstream reaction hazards; lack of current configuration does not justify noncompliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA is unconvinced that software issues pose an obstacle; software vendors can update systems and many downstream hazards are already classified elsewhere (example: formaldehyde by-product). The agency notes absence of evidence of technological barriers.

rubrics_metrics.name: OSHA's rejection of tort-liability expansion claims
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA finds no merit in arguments that updating paragraph (d)(1) would expand tort liability for manufacturers, noting the OSH Act preserves workers' compensation and other legal rights without expanding liability via this rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No commenters provided case law or evidence to support tort-liability expansion claims; OSHA cites 29 U.S.C. 653(b)(4) to explain statutory limits on rule's effect on other legal liabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: OSHA's approach to address out-of-scope suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggestions outside the rulemaking scope (e.g., providing authoritative classification lists or adding the 'single study rule') will not be adopted in this rule; they are addressed elsewhere (Appendix F, past preambles) or are out of scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA summarizes why certain stakeholder proposals are outside the specific changes being made and points to other HCS materials where related topics are addressed.
